title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 4: The Centenary and the Academe
keywords: Retired Justice Ameurfina Melencio A. Herrera
UP Law Dean Merlin M. Magallona
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- a speech CJP delivered at the noncompetitive Centennial Debate between Ateneo de Manila and Silliman University on February 9, 2001 in Dumaguete City, explaining the four centenary programs aimed at the academe (law schools and law students)

Four legal-education programs: (1) the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education (P50M endowment for national professorial chairs and scholarships for poor law students); (2) a Special Committee on Legal Education (curriculum and bar-exam reform); (3) a national moot court competition; and (4) a National Speech Festival of debates, oratorical and essay contests

The argument that mastery of language is the most basic requirement for lawyers: language as a 'time binder' that lets humanity transmit discovery (Mendel, Einstein), and the indispensable forensic and writing skills of the legal profession
An editorial bracket recording the actual contest winners (Oratorical, Debate, Essay) and the noncompetitive nature of the Dumaguete debate
sub_topics: The Dumaguete debate setting: eight debaters (four Ateneans, four Sillimanians) at Luce Auditorium before 800 who paid P50 admission -- 'I thought such an aberration would happen only during PBA basketball games or during concerts of Regine Velasquez'; CJP attended as guest speaker, not judge; board of judges: Sen. Franklin Drilon ('who chose dignity and integrity over position and possessions'), Rep. Jacinto Paras, Dr. Henry Sojor

Centenary goals restated: first, to communicate the judiciary's nation-building role; second, to encourage participation in the ongoing judicial reform program; overall theme 'Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman'

Program 1 -- the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education (chaired by Atty. Ricardo J. Romulo): the Court commits a P10M seed fund and the Foundation raises P40M (P50M total endowment) for national professorial chairs and fellowships/scholarships for deserving but poor law students; aim to provide adequately paid full-time professors (comparable to AIM pay) to schools that cannot afford them

Program 2 -- a Special Committee on Legal Education (chaired by Justice Jose C. Vitug) reviewing the law curriculum, with a corollary group under retired Justice Ameurfina Melencio A. Herrera reforming the bar examinations

Program 3 -- a national moot court competition under a sub-committee headed by former UP Law Dean Merlin M. Magallona; guidelines available through PIO Atty. Ismael G. Khan Jr.; regional contests leading to a Manila final

Program 4 -- a National Speech Festival (debates, oratorical and essay contests) co-sponsored by the Philippine Association of Law Schools, supervised by former Law Dean and Justice Secretary Hernando B. Perez (vice chair Dean Ponciano Subido), with FEU Dean Andres Bautista (essay), MLQ Dean Norberto Gonzales (oratory) and UP Dean Raul Pangalangan (debate); 75 law schools from 9 regions participating

Editorial bracket recording the results: National Oratorical Contest -- Claude Albert Morales (UP) champion, Andre A. Fornier (Ateneo) first runner-up, Cynette Lovelyn Mirasol (San Agustin) second; National Debate -- Xavier University champion, UP runner-up; Essay Contest -- Margarita Victorino (FEU) first, Jan Kendrick Velasco (FEU) second, Adrian Montemayor (UST) third

The decision to make the Dumaguete dual meet a special centenary feature, with cash prizes for best speaker, best debater and best rebuttal speaker plus transportation and lodging stipends for visiting debaters

stances.claim: Mastery of language is the single most basic requirement for entering the legal profession -- 'a student who does not have a singular command of communication skills has no place in the noble profession of law' -- because language is a 'time binder' that allows humanity to transmit discovery and render justice; in no other profession is the command of language more critical.
stances.rhetorical_move: language-as-time-binder argument: elevating communication skill from a soft attribute to the defining competency of law, illustrated by Mendel and Einstein transmitting lifetimes of discovery in hours
stances.confidence: asserted as a governing claim about the legal profession

stances.claim: Elevating legal education is a core part of judicial reform, and the Court must actively underwrite it -- through an endowment that pays full-time professors (at AIM-comparable rates) to schools 'that cannot afford to hire them on their own meager resources,' so that the rest of the country can 'teach law in a grand manner' as Ateneo and Silliman already do. Equalizing access to quality legal education is an institutional responsibility, not merely a private-school achievement.
stances.rhetorical_move: education-equalization-as-reform: framing professorial chairs and scholarships as redistributive judicial-reform machinery rather than charity
stances.confidence: asserted as the rationale for the four academe programs

notable_anecdotes: The paid debate audience: CJP marvels that 800 people paid P50 each to watch a law-school debate at Luce Auditorium -- 'I thought such an aberration would happen only during PBA basketball games or during concerts of Regine Velasquez' -- his evidence that forensic competition can capture the public.

Recusing from judging: he is 'glad that I did not have to act as judge, but only as guest speaker,' since judging would force him to disappoint some debaters; he reserves judgment for when these debaters 'appear as lawyers in the Supreme Court.'

The P50M endowment design: the Court seeds P10M and the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education (chaired by Ricardo Romulo) raises P40M, the income to pay national professorial chairs at rates comparable to Asian Institute of Management professors -- a concrete mechanism to lift under-resourced law schools.

Language as a time binder: it took Mendel a lifetime to discover dominant and recessive characteristics and Einstein a lifetime for relativity, 'but because Mendel and Einstein recorded their knowledge in clear, precise language, their discoveries can be explained... in just a matter of hours.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the speech CJP gave at the noncompetitive Centennial Debate between Ateneo de Manila and Silliman University on February 9, 2001 in Dumaguete City, where 800 people paid P50 each to watch eight debaters at Luce Auditorium -- 'I thought such an aberration would happen only during PBA basketball games or during concerts of Regine Velasquez.' Glad to attend as guest speaker rather than judge (he reserves judgment for when the debaters 'appear as lawyers in the Supreme Court'), he uses the occasion to explain four centenary programs aimed at the academe. First, the Foundation for the Enhancement of Legal Education (chaired by Atty. Ricardo J. Romulo): the Court seeds P10 million and the Foundation raises P40 million for a P50-million endowment funding national professorial chairs and scholarships for poor law students, paying full-time professors at rates comparable to the Asian Institute of Management so under-resourced schools can 'teach law in a grand manner' as Ateneo and Silliman do. Second, a Special Committee on Legal Education under Justice Jose C. Vitug reviewing the curriculum, with a corollary group under retired Justice Ameurfina Melencio A. Herrera reforming the bar examinations. Third, a national moot court competition under former UP Law Dean Merlin M. Magallona. Fourth, a National Speech Festival of debates, oratorical and essay contests co-sponsored by the Philippine Association of Law Schools and supervised by Justice Secretary Hernando B. Perez, with 75 law schools from 9 regions participating (an editorial bracket records the winners: UP's Claude Albert Morales in oratory, Xavier University in debate, and FEU's Margarita Victorino in the essay contest). His governing thesis is that mastery of language is the most basic requirement of lawyering -- 'a student who does not have a singular command of communication skills has no place in the noble profession of law' -- because 'language is a time binder' that let Mendel and Einstein transmit lifetimes of discovery 'in just a matter of hours.' He closes wishing the debaters to 'become the competent and ethical lawyers that you aspire to be.'
